3	# A generic declaration beside a plain one: the judgement
4	
5	The question is PLAN item 30 (row 496). Answer 9 lets a name have a generic declaration and a plain one. When the checker sends a call to the plain one and the value at run time also fits the generic one, which declaration runs, and at which instance? The clean worker's list (`reviews/plain-beside-generic-ways.md`, "the list" below) gives five ways with their measurements. This note checks its deciding claims against their sources, weighs the ways, and recommends one.
6	
7	## 1. The question, in plain words
8	
9	Terms first.
10	
11	- A *declaration* (an "arm") is one definition of a name. A *generic* declaration has static parameters, `grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])`; a *plain* one has none, `grab(a: Any)`.
12	- The *static choice* is the declaration the checker picks from the declared types. *Dispatch* is the choice made at run time from the values' actual types: Fortress runs the most specific declaration that fits the values. Java does not do this; Julia does.
13	- An *instance* of a generic declaration is the declaration at one value of its parameters, `grab` at `X = Red`. On the compiled path each instance is a class stamped from a template.
14	
15	The shape. `grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\]): Marker[\X\]` beside `grab(a: Any): Any`, and a call `grab(a)` where `a` is declared `Any` and holds a `RedTag`, which is a `Tag[\Red\]`. The checker picks the plain declaration, the only one whose declared domain holds `Any`. At run time the generic one fits too, and it is narrower. Two things are asked: which declaration runs, and if the generic one, what `X` is.
16	
17	Why the question exists. Fortress keeps generics at run time (the instantiating loader, type descriptors, sizes as descriptors since batch 5) and dispatches on the run-time types of all arguments. A language that erases generics and resolves overloads statically cannot ask this; both design choices are the team's.
18	
19	## 2. The list's deciding claims, checked
20	
21	Each claim, the source opened, the verdict.
22	
23	1. **Every source that speaks gives the generic declaration, at the instance the values fix.** The 2011 Types paper names the case: "If d2 is the most specific declaration applicable to the static types of the argument expressions, and d1 ≤ d2 is the most specific declaration applicable to the ilks of the arguments, then ... Because the call is dispatched to d1, we require type parameters for d1 to be inferred dynamically" (`Papers/Types/rules.tick:118-129`; an ilk is a value's run-time type). Its applicability: "A function declaration is applicable to a type if and only if at least one of its instances is" (`setup.tick:393-397`), a plain declaration being the degenerate case (`introduction.tick:320-331`). Welterweight (2012) instantiates each candidate by the substitution that places the run-time types in its domain (`Papers/Welterweight/fig-msa.tick`, the rules `Applicable` and `MSAV-Standard`), its dispatch semipredicate "returns ... a set of type bindings for the static type parameters of that entrypoint" (`dispatch.tick:20`), and "inference also aims to obtain the most specific instantiation of an applicable entrypoint" (`:67`). X must be Object" (`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/2012-6-15 return type instantiation restrictions.txt:70-77`; his declaration names the parameter `P` and his prose `X`). 138	
139	**Question.** When a name has a generic declaration and a plain one, and a call the checker sent to the plain one carries a value that fits the generic one, which runs, and at which type?
140	
141	**Context.**
142	
143	- Refresher. There are two choices. The checker chooses from declared types (the static choice). At run time Fortress chooses again from the values' actual types and runs the narrowest declaration that fits, on all arguments; Java never does this, Julia always does. A generic declaration is a family: `grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])` fits every `Tag`, and the value says which `X`.
144	- The shape. `grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])` beside `grab(a: Any)`, called `grab(a)` with `a` declared `Any` and holding a `RedTag`. The checker picks the plain one, the only one that takes `Any`. At run time the generic one fits too and is narrower.

146	- What the paths do. Both were built for the generic answer. The compiled path gives it in the team's own gated test and in seven of ours; rung G's two programs crash on two code-generation slips (a `ZZ32` spelled two ways; a cast to the wrong class), not because the plain one was chosen. 147	- What the library does. Every list and map comprehension joins its pieces through exactly this shape (`APPCOV`, whose plain declaration is a deliberate `fail`), and the pair `=` sits beside the `Any` `=`. The plain answer breaks both.
148	- Your decision of this morning (conversions and overloading, decision 1) already says which declaration: dispatch goes "to the most specific declaration applicable to the values", and a generic one fits "when some instance within its bounds fits". 149	- microGPT has no such pair.

151	
152	**Options.**
153	
154	1. Touches: one sentence and one example in 7b's rung S; about 5 lines in walk (rung W) with a test, closing row 157; two expected-failure compiled tests in rung C for the two crashes, which stay on phase 5's code-generation list. Costs: no new rung, no probe, no gated test changes.
155	2. The plain declaration runs: a generic declaration is dispatched only with the call's own static arguments, and a call sent to the plain one has none. Touches: 3 lines in the code generator; a specification sentence against your decision 1; a redesign of the covariant collections and the pair `=`. Costs: 8 gated compiled tests go red; walk cannot follow, having no static types, so the two paths split on every such call; what runs depends on a variable's declared type, not on its value.

157	4. Refuse such a call. Refuses the library's own bodies, every generic body that calls `=` on a type parameter. Listed for completeness.
158

162	
163	**Recommendation.** Option 1: the generic declaration runs at the instance the value fixes; one sentence in rung S, row 157's fix in rung W, two expected-failure tests in rung C.

- Rung S rewrites `advanced/overloading.tex`, which holds P2. Without your answer it names row 491 among the passages it leaves (`PLAN.md`, batch 7b's line).

- Answer 9 revises the chapter to the 2011 paper's rules. The paper's Meet rule asks for the meet as a type. Way 2 adds the coverage form beside it. I read that as an extension, since answer 9 is about static parameters, but the record should say so.
- Once row 492 is repaired, a call whose static type is in between has two minimal candidates.
  - The checker takes the head of a sort (`Functionals.scala:462`), and Welterweight wants exactly one.
  - Rung C meets this shape. It exists since 2009 through a trait with a clause of its own (`OwnClauseBetween`).

- Row 491, a note: the own-clause case breaks P1 at the level of types too, with no static parameters, on the compiled path since 2009 (`OwnClauseBetween`). Candidate (b) is not sufficient (`OneClosedBetween`).
- A candidate row: top-level abstract function declarations refused by both paths.
  - Walk refuses at `BuildEnvironments.java:292`.

cd /home/user/fortress/explorations/compile-ladder/plan-7b && python3 - <<'EOF'
p='CLIMB-BATCH-7.draft.md'; s=open(p).read()
a=s.index("**Item 30, a generic declaration beside a plain one at run time (rows 496 and 499).**")
b=s.index("**Read from the record, not asked.**")
new = """**Item 30. When a name has a generic declaration and a plain one, and a call the checker sent to the plain one carries a value that fits the generic one, which runs, and at which type?** Row 496. A top-tier judgement recommends option 1 (`explorations/reviews/plain-beside-generic-judgement.md`, from the clean worker's list, `reviews/plain-beside-generic-ways.md`). This record takes option 1 as the batch's default and does not answer the question; it is yours, in the judgement's section "For Pavol".
- A refresher. The checker chooses a declaration from the declared types. At run time Fortress chooses again from the values' actual types and runs the narrowest declaration that fits; Java never does this, Julia always does. A generic declaration is a family: `grab[\\X\\](t: Tag[\\X\\])` fits every `Tag`, and the value says which `X`.
- The shape: `grab[\\X\\](t: Tag[\\X\\])` beside `grab(a: Any)`, called `grab(a)` with `a` declared `Any` and holding a `Tag[\\Red\\]`. The checker picks the plain one. At run time the generic one fits too, and it is narrower.
- Which declaration runs is already settled by your decision of 2026-09-28 on conversions and overloading (decision 1): dispatch goes to the most specific declaration applicable to the values, and a generic one is applicable when some instance within its bounds fits. Only one sentence is new: at which instance a declaration reached only at run time runs.
- What the designers said: the 2011 paper names this case and gives the generic declaration, its parameter inferred at run time; the 2012 calculus, the restart and Naden's 2012 notes say the same; no source gives the plain one. What the paths do: both were built for the generic answer (the team's gated test `Compiled12.invariantInference` among eight). Rung G's two programs crash on two code-generation slips, and walk's one "plain" answer is a 2007 bug, row 157. The library relies on it: every list and map comprehension joins its pieces through this shape (`APPCOV`), and so does the pair `=`. microGPT has no such pair. (The judgement, sections 1 and 2.)
- The options, in the judgement's words:
  1. **The generic declaration runs, at the instance the value fixes**: unique wherever the parameter sits inside a parameter's type, else the least instance within its bounds (the 2012 calculus's rule). Touches: one sentence and one example in rung S; about 5 lines in walk with a test, closing row 157, in rung W; two expected-failure compiled tests in rung C for the two crashes, which stay on phase 5's code-generation list. No new rung, no probe, no gated test changes.
  2. **The plain declaration runs**: a generic declaration is dispatched only with the call's own static arguments. Costs 8 gated compiled tests going red, a sentence against your decision 1, a redesign of the covariant collections and the pair `=`, and a split between the paths, since walk has no static types.
  3. **Refuse the pair at the declaration.** Reverses part of answer 9, and refuses the library's `APPCOV`, pair `=` and the eight tests.
  4. **Refuse such a call.** Refuses the library's own bodies. Listed for completeness.
- A yes to (1) commits you to this record as amended in S, W and C, and to two defaults listed for your review: the least instance where the value does not fix it, and Naden's return-type restriction recorded as future work, not built. Row 496 moves to home 2 and closes in phase 5. The case where nothing fixes the parameter (row 446, item 17) stays yours and comes on its own.
- What the batch does if no answer comes before the launch: (1), the judgement's recommendation. Under another answer the coordinator rewrites S's, W's and C's answers lines and the text they mark before the launch.
- **Recommended by the judgement: (1).**

"""
s=s[:a]+new+s[b:]
open(p,'w').write(s)
print('ok')
EOF

3	# The passages that read `comprises` at the level of types: the judgement
4	
5	The question. Climb batch 7C rewrote the traits chapter to the type group's 2012 reading of a `comprises` clause: the clause says to which types a trait's values belong, and a trait with static parameters may stand unlisted between a closed trait and its listed types when every trait or object extending it is below a listed type (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:235-252`). Four passages elsewhere still argue from a clause at the level of types: the intersection example (P1, `basic/types-vals-vars.tex:583-604`), the Meet Rule's example (P2, `advanced/overloading.tex:275-307`), the rule on abstract function declarations (P3, `basic/functions.tex:370-415`) and a team draft note (P4, `basic/components/source-code.tex:428-434`). Row 491 asks whether they still hold and what the specification and the two implementations should do. The clean worker's note (`reviews/comprises-type-level-ways.md`, "the ways note" below) lists six ways and marks its own reading. This note checks the deciding claims at their sources, adds one measurement, weighs the ways and recommends one.
6	
7	## 1. The type question, in plain words
8	
9	Terms first.
10	
11	- `trait S comprises { U, V }` closes `S`. The type reading: every type under `S` is under `U` or `V`. This was the Working Draft's note and it is Java's `sealed`. The value reading, "coverage": every value of `S` is a value of `U` or `V`. This is the 2012 Types chapter and Welterweight, and batch 7C's text. A trait has no values of its own; only objects make values. So under the value reading a trait may sit between `S` and its listed types, and it is a type below `S` and below no listed type.
12	- P1 and P2 conclude "any subtype of both S and T must be a subtype of V. Thus, V = S ∩ T" from the clauses of `S` and `T` and `U excludes W`. That first step needs the type reading. Under the value reading the same steps show that every value of both `S` and `T` is a value of `V`: `V` covers `S ∩ T`.
13	- P3 and P4 speak of "every immediate subtype" of a closed trait. Under the type reading those are the listed types. Under 7C's text they can differ: `AnyIntegral`'s immediate subtype is `Integral[\I\]`, its listed types the five integer types.
